claims.text: Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles contain local fluctuations in chemical order.
Local chemical-order fluctuations create regions with different local cohesive energies.
Heterogeneous cohesive-energy regions govern the premelting and melting behavior of these nanoparticles.
The Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu nanoparticles are initially solid and compositionally uniform at the particle scale.
Size-matched mono- or bimetallic nanoparticles can serve as the chemically simpler baseline.
The HEA and baseline particles will receive identical thermal exposure under a controlled atmosphere.
A statistically random elemental distribution in the HEA produces local variations in bonding strength and cohesive energy.
Regions of lower cohesive energy act as nucleation sites for premature surface melting.
Nucleation at heterogeneous low-cohesive-energy regions produces a broad onset of phase change.
Uniformly structured baseline nanoparticles undergo a sharper and more collective melting transition.
The HEA nanoparticles will begin surface premelting earlier than the baseline particles.
The HEA nanoparticles will exhibit a more gradual premelting onset than the baseline particles.
Spatially resolved measurements will reveal localized melting regions in the HEA nanoparticles.
The baseline nanoparticles will display a single sharp melting point.
Mono- or bimetallic baseline nanoparticles melt more uniformly because their composition is homogeneous.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply to near-equiatomic HEA nanoparticles approximately 5–50 nm in size and prepared under similar synthesis conditions.
Larger particles or particles with significant elemental segregation may not follow the proposed behavior.
A correlation between local chemical order and spatially varying melting onset is required by the proposed mechanism.
